Garmite
GAR-mite
n. (the designation of Keilah in the genealogies of Judah; named once)
A gentilic of uncertain origin, Hebrew Garmi, perhaps from gerem, a bone, and so bony or strong; used once, 1 Chronicles 4:19.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Garmite occurs once, in the crowded Judahite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4: “And the sons of his wife Hodiah the sister of Naham, the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite” (1 Chronicles 4:19). Keilah is also the name of a town in Judah that David once delivered from the Philistines and whose men would have given him up to Saul; here the name belongs to a man, or is used of the clan that held the town, which is the ordinary way of these registers. The chapter is a thicket of names, and the Authorized Version's margin notes Jehudijah as an alternative for Hodiah, the same woman named in the verse before: “And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah” (1 Chronicles 4:18). In the middle of these lists stands one of the best-known prayers in Scripture: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Garmite, the designation of Keilah in the Judahite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4.

expand to see more

Garmite is a gentilic of uncertain derivation.

Some connect it with gerem, a bone, and render it bony or strong.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at 1 Chronicles 4:19.

It designates Keilah, named in the genealogies of Judah.

Keilah is also a town of Judah delivered by David from the Philistines.

Key Scripture

1Ch 4:19 — "And the sons of his wife Hodiah the sister of Naham, the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite."

1Ch 4:18 — "And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took."

1Ch 4:10 — "And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested."

Num 26:55 — "Notwithstanding the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit."

Modern Corruption

Jabez's prayer is lifted out of this genealogy and sold as a formula for material increase, where the man asks chiefly to be kept from evil.

expand to see more

The chapter that gives us the Garmite is best known for a prayer that has been detached from it, printed on its own, and marketed as a method for obtaining prosperity. The prayer itself has four petitions, and the weight falls on the last two: that God's hand might be with him, and that he might be kept from evil so that it would not grieve him. Enlarging a coast, in a book about tribal inheritance, means receiving what God has promised, not acquiring what a man has coveted. A petition torn from its register and turned into a technique has been made to say the opposite of what it says.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God hears obscure men in the middle of long lists. Jabez has two verses between two columns of names, and the chapter records plainly that God granted him what he asked. That is the encouragement a reader is meant to take from a genealogy.
